abstract: Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) can noninvasively modulate neural activity in the human brain (Blackmore et al., 2019; Fomenko et al., 2018; Legon et al., 2014), and EEG, with millisecond resolution, is well suited to track the timing of cortical engagement. In humans, tFUS aimed at primary visual cortex (V1) has been reported to evoke phosphenes, with EEG peaks (N55, P100) during sonication (Lee et al., 2016). Ultrasound can also activate cortex indirectly through the auditory pathway (Sato et al., 2018), although airborne sound from the transducer can be masked (Braun et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2023). Whether the N55 and P100 peaks reflect neuronal activation or artifacts (i.e., non-neuronal signals produced by the ultrasound itself) is unclear. We set out to ask whether EEG decoding could detect neural engagement during tFUS to V1 in eight participants receiving 150 or 300-ms pulses or sham. Decoding of tFUS versus sham reached as much as 93% for exactly the duration of each pulse (cluster p = .004 and .008), with no later cluster significant. But the same pulse-locked step appeared on all channels, scaled with drive, and was also recorded from a foam head and a forehead piezo pickup, identifying it as mechanical. Decoding during sonication must therefore be interpreted as a mechanical artifact rather than cortical engagement. EEG peaks observed within a pulse cannot on their own be taken as evidence of neural engagement. EEG studies of tFUS will need controls that reproduce the vibration without focusing on the brain, such as an active sham.
